title: xflow-exporter
description: NetFlow, IPFIX and sFlow received by xflow-exporter, ranked by packets. Flow export is sampled, so every packet and byte figure is an estimate scaled by the sampling rate; take an exact volume from the device's SNMP interface counters. What flow export gives that SNMP cannot is the dimensions: AS, protocol, application, peer. Rollup sets the rate window -- pick one at least twice the scrape interval or every panel reads empty. The composition panels rank rather than total.

panels.title: Devices heard from
panels.description: Devices whose datagrams have decoded at least once. The series appears on the first successful decode and never on a device that has only ever failed.

panels.title: Longest silence
panels.description: Time since the most stale device last had a datagram decode. Every counter a silent device feeds is frozen, which rate() reports as zero, so this is the only signal that separates a silent device from a quiet network.

panels.title: Receive queue
panels.description: How full the bounded receive queue is. A queue that reaches its capacity drops datagrams, counted under reason=queue_full.

panels.title: Build
panels.description: The running version, from xflow_build_info.

panels.title: Datagrams received
panels.description: Per listener. This counts datagrams off the wire, before any decoding, so it rises even while every packet is being refused.

panels.title: Datagrams dropped
panels.description: Anything here is loss the exporter caused rather than the network: queue_full is the receive queue overrunning, truncated is a datagram larger than the read buffer.

panels.title: Decode errors
panels.description: By reason. missing_template is ordinary for a while after a device or exporter restart and must stop rising once the device re-announces; invalid_template is a template this exporter refused to compile.

panels.title: Export packets lost
panels.description: Gaps the export sequence numbers say happened between this exporter and the device. The flows in a lost packet are gone: no counter here can recover them.

panels.title: Templates held
panels.description: Unexpired templates per observation domain. A data template arrives before the options templates do, so an options count of zero shortly after startup is ordinary.

panels.title: Packet rate
panels.description: Sampling-corrected packets per second. Under 1-in-N packet sampling this is an estimate scaled by N, not a measurement: read it for shape and proportion. An exact volume comes from the device's SNMP interface counters, which this exporter does not and cannot replace.

panels.title: Flow records received
panels.description: As exported, with no sampling multiplication: a packet-sampling protocol observes flows, it does not count them. This is the rate the device is telling you things at, and it bounds how much statistical weight every other panel has.

panels.title: Sampling rate in force
panels.description: The divisor every packet and byte figure above was multiplied by. Absent until an options template announces one, and while it is absent the figures are uncorrected -- a device sampling 1-in-N then under-reports by N.

panels.title: Mean packet size
panels.description: Bytes divided by packets. A ratio survives sampling far better than either half of it does, because the scale factor cancels. Small and steady is signalling, DNS or voice; large is bulk transfer; a fall with the packet rate rising is the shape scanning and floods make.

panels.title: Packets per flow record
panels.description: How much each record summarises. A device that reports one record per sampled packet sits at the sampling rate; higher means its cache is aggregating. A collapse toward one, with the record rate climbing, is many short-lived flows -- a scan or a flood.

panels.title: Mean packet size by protocol
panels.description: The same ratio split by transport. The protocols separate cleanly by size, so a shift here is a change in what the traffic is, not in how much of it there is.

panels.title: Composition -- ranked by packets, Top-K views rather than totals
Protocol mix
panels.description: Packets per second by transport. Ranking by packets rather than by bytes answers a different question, and on real traffic the two orders differ: an AS sending many small packets can lead here and be absent from the byte ranking entirely.

panels.title: Top AS by packets
panels.description: Who is sending the most packets, which is not who is sending the most bytes. Filled by the device where it exports AS numbers, by --enrich.asn-database where it does not, and a zero is a side no database placed -- a private address never will be.

panels.title: Top applications by packets
panels.description: The service view worth reading. A device exports both directions, so the return half of a download keys on the client's ephemeral port -- four fifths of all bytes on one measured link -- and only --enrich.services resolves either side to a name.

panels.title: Top conversations by packets
panels.description: Address pairs ranked by packet rate. Entries below --aggregation.top-k publish nothing, and the other series carries only what the entry bound folded at ingest, so this ranks rather than totals.

panels.title: Top destination services by packets
panels.description: What each service received, summed over every host that reached it. Directional rather than a host total: with ingress observation at two points the two directions of one conversation are separate entries.

targets.expr: topk(10, sum by (exporter, dst, proto, port) (rate(xflow_destination_packets_total{exporter=~"$exporter"}[$rollup_interval])))

panels.title: Country pairs by packets
panels.description: The country each prefix is REGISTERED in, not where the traffic went. An anycast prefix answers from a different continent depending on who asks -- a lab in Japan reaching Cloudflare measured src_country=CA. Do not reconcile this with a transit bill.

panels.title: Traffic touching a flagged address
panels.description: Only addresses a threat list names appear here, and the side is kept: a hit on src is an outside address reaching in, a hit on dst is an inside host that reached a listed one. An empty panel is the expected state of a clean network, not a broken lookup.

panels.title: Volume -- a sampled estimate, read as proportion
Estimated throughput
panels.description: Sampling-corrected bytes, scaled by the sampling rate. Under 1-in-N sampling a byte figure carries the variance of the packet-size distribution on top of the counting error, so it is the noisiest thing here in absolute terms. The proportions between series hold up; the absolute number does not. Take an exact volume from the device's SNMP interface counters.

panels.title: Byte share by AS
panels.description: The same AS pairs weighted by bytes rather than packets. Compare with the packet ranking above: a large-packet source leads here and can be missing there, and the difference is the point of having both.

panels.title: Flow size distribution
panels.description: Native histograms, published only with --collector.distributions and read only by a Prometheus scraping with native histograms enabled. Absent otherwise.

panels.title: Entries held
panels.description: Per table. Compare with --aggregation.max-entries: a table sitting at the bound is refusing new keys, and with --aggregation.top-k to see how much of it reaches a series at all.

panels.title: Records folded at the entry bound
panels.description: The saturation signal. Anything above zero means the table is full and new keys are being folded into other instead of getting a series. Raise --aggregation.max-entries.

panels.title: Entries evicted
panels.description: Idle entries whose series disappeared. Ordinary churn; the totals they carried are not folded into other, because a published entry's bytes were already counted there.

panels.title: Enrichment lookups
panels.description: Per source. filled is a dimension the device omitted and the source supplied, unknown is a source that had no answer, skipped is a dimension the device had already carried.

panels.title: Refusals
panels.description: Bounds the wire cannot exceed. Each is a device, or an attacker, being held to a budget: a refused announcement is a name that falls back to its number, a refused domain is one the per-device budget turned away.

panels.title: Flagged addresses held
panels.description: Addresses the threat lists name. Zero with --enrich.threat-file set means the file loaded nothing.

panels.title: Threat list lines skipped
panels.description: Lines that named no address, a list published in CIDR notation being the usual reason. Those addresses are not covered, which is absence rather than a clean bill of health.

panels.title: Threat list reload failures
panels.description: A failed reload keeps the previous set, so a missing file never unflags every address at once. The database enrichers behave the same way.
